title: NOAA GFS — forecast from an Icechunk repository
description: Two metres of air temperature from the newest GFS run, stepping forward hour by hour. The archive is an Icechunk repository, which no Zarr reader can open on its own: the server resolves it and answers in tiles.

options.content:
Air temperature two metres above the ground, from the most recent run of NOAA's Global Forecast System, hour by hour out to two days.

The map draws the hour at the **end** of the dashboard's range, and the range runs into the future — `now+2d` — because a forecast does. Narrow it to walk the forecast, or press play on the map's own time bar; if you do, switch that bar's window mode to *incremental*, because in the default *free* mode the window is as wide as the whole forecast and slides without ever changing which hour is drawn.

The archive is published by dynamical.org as an **Icechunk** repository. Chunk objects there are named by opaque identifiers and the map from array coordinates to object lives in a manifest, so a browser cannot fetch a chunk even knowing exactly which one it wants — it would have to read the manifests first, and the library that does that will not run in a Grafana page. The tile server resolves the repository instead, which is why the store address below starts with `stac+`: the catalogue is asked where the repository is today, rather than the address being written down and going stale on the next version.

A tile over Ecuador costs about two seconds; the whole world at zoom 0 costs about thirty. That is the archive's shape showing through — it is chunked for reading a long time series at one place, so a map pays for 105 forecast hours to draw one.

panels.title: 2 m temperature · newest GFS run · the hour drawn is the end of the range

targets.rawSql:
-- Una fila por hora del pronostico. DuckDB no lee Icechunk y no lo intenta:
-- aqui solo se calcula QUE pedir, y el servidor de teselas lo resuelve.
--
-- La pasada: GFS arranca cada 6 h y dynamical tarda un rato en ingerirla, asi
-- que se toma el ultimo multiplo de 6 h que tenga ya 9 horas de antiguedad. Es
-- margen, no precision: pedir una pasada que aun no esta da teselas vacias.
WITH run AS (
  SELECT to_timestamp(floor(epoch(now() - INTERVAL '9 hours') / 21600) * 21600) AS init
)
SELECT
  init + INTERVAL '1 hour' * h AS time,
  -- `stac+` en vez de la url del bucket: dynamical rueda la version del
  -- repositorio (`v0.2.7` hoy) y pide que nadie la fije. El servidor pregunta
  -- al catalogo donde esta hoy.
  'stac+https://stac.dynamical.org/noaa-gfs-forecast/collection.json' AS zarr_url,
  'temperature_2m' AS zarr_variable,
  -- El reloj recorre `lead_time`, no `time`: el archivo es un cubo de
  -- pronostico y su eje temporal son dos, la pasada y el salto.
  'lead_time' AS zarr_time_dim,
  -- TRAMPA: el eje es `timedelta64[us]` pero el valor va en NANOSEGUNDOS.
  -- TiTiler convierte la cadena con el tipo escalar generico de numpy y pandas
  -- la interpreta en ns pase lo que pase; en microsegundos no encuentra nada y
  -- responde 500 «not all values found in index».
  (h * 3600 * 1000000000)::BIGINT::VARCHAR AS zarr_time_label,
  -- La pasada se fija, en el formato numpy de siempre.
  'init_time=' || strftime(init AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.000000000') AS zarr_sel
FROM run, generate_series(0, 48) g(h)
ORDER BY time
